## Claims — grouped by pericope

### 1:20–23 (§III B — God's power raising and enthroning Christ over the powers)
- **[1:20–23]** Thielman's framing: the section explains how God applied his power "for us who believe" (v.19). "God's power raised Christ from the dead and seated him, victorious, at God's right hand, with all enemy forces conquered and beneath Christ's feet (1:20–22a). God has also given Christ to the church in his capacity as victorious, authoritative head over all these forces (1:22b–23)." (Thielman, l.10)
- **[1:20]** Function/structure: the passage provides the "transition from the letter's prayer section into the letter's main theological discussion in chapters 2 and 3." (Thielman, l.12) Grammatically continues the sentence from v.15; NA27/most translations start new sentence at v.20, losing "the run-on quality of Paul's language and therefore the emotional engagement." (Thielman, l.14)
- **[1:20]** Terminology is "a skillful blend of language from Israel's Scriptures and language from the Greco-Roman environment." Paul uses Pss. 110:1 (109:1 LXX) and 8:6 (8:7 MT/LXX): as the LORD gave the king military victory (Ps 110) and subjected creation to humans (Ps 8), "so God has given his anointed king Jesus, the Messiah, victory over all forces ranged against him." (Thielman, l.20)
- **[1:20]** The heavenly-powers terminology uses terms that "in the religious environment of his readers typically referred to the gods who were thought to control the fate of human beings and the destiny of nations." Fear of such powers was common. (Thielman, l.20)
- **[1:20]** Ps. 110:1 "probably played a role in first-century debates about the identity of the Messiah even beyond Christian circles" (cites Moritz 1996a); NT interest usually lies in Jesus's exaltation/vindication (cites Hay 1973). (Thielman, l.32)
- **[1:20]** Thielman's view: Paul's "chief concern in alluding to the psalm lies not in the location of the king at God's right hand, but in God's defeat of the king's enemies in the second half of the verse (Ps. 110:1b)" — the part Paul does not explicitly quote. (Thielman, l.34)
- **[1:20]** *en tois epouraniois* ("in the heavenly places") = "a blanket term describing the 'dimension' in which all spiritual powers exist, whether good (1:3; cf. 2:6) or inimical (6:12)." (cites W.H. Harris 1991, Hanson 1980) (Thielman, l.36)
- **[1:21]** The list *pasēs archēs kai exousias kai dynameōs kai kyriotētos kai pantos onomatos onomazomenou* ("all rule and authority and power and lordship and every name that is named") — the position *hyperanō* ("high above") in a Ps 110 context "shows that they are inimical powers and that God has given the Messiah Jesus victory over them." (Thielman, l.38) Likely includes both demonic forces controlled through magic (cites Arnold 1989, 1995) and "the alliance between present earthly political rulers and the deities of the transcendent realm." (Thielman, l.40)
- **[1:21]** *ou monon en tō aiōni toutō alla kai en tō mellonti* — this two-ages contrast is "the only place in the Pauline corpus where the full contrast between the two ages is explicitly expressed." (Thielman, l.40) Position dispute: some (Lindemann, Schnackenburg, Best) say no real future age is meant — just traditional language emphasizing completeness; others (O'Brien, Hoehner, Sellin) say Ephesians still affirms future completion (1:10, 14; 2:7; 4:30; 5:27; 6:8, 11–12). (Thielman, l.42)
- **[1:21]** Greco-Roman-context reading (Thielman's own emphasis): imperial coins/inscriptions/calendar tempted readers to think time was organized around Rome's eternal authority. Cites an excavated Ephesian house graffito: "Rome, the ruler of all, your power will never die," and a Decree of Assos (AD 37): "the most pleasant age for humanity that is now present." Paul counters that God organized time around Christ (1:10), who holds authority "both now and forever." (Thielman, l.44)
- **[1:22a]** Paul supplements Ps 110:1 with a paraphrase of Ps 8:6, as in 1 Cor 15:25–27 and like 1 Pet 3:22; Heb 1:3,13; 2:6–8. (Thielman, l.46) Thielman: Paul may have had all of Ps 8 in mind — human beings "a little lower than God," "crowned with glory and honor," given "dominion" — but "his point is different than that of the psalm": the divine/human sovereignty the psalm and Roman ideology (Augustus) located in humanity, "Paul finds instead in the Messiah Jesus." (Thielman, l.48)
- **[1:22b]** *kai auton edōken kephalēn hyper panta tē ekklēsia* ("and he gave him as head over all things to the church"). (Thielman, l.50)
- **[1:22b]** *ekklēsia*: primarily a political assembly in Greek; LXX used it for "the assembly [qāhāl] of the LORD." Since Paul didn't think of the church as political and ekklēsia wasn't the obvious Roman term for a club (cites Wilken 1984), "he probably reflects the use of the word in the LXX" and thought of the multiethnic church "as, in some sense, continuous with the 'assembly of the LORD' in Israel's Scriptures." (Thielman, l.52) Theodoret glosses the church as "the collection [syllogos] of the faithful." (cites R. Hill 2001) (Thielman, l.52)
- **[1:22b]** *ekklēsia* here = universal church (prominent in the disputed later letters, but with precedent in undisputed letters 1 Cor 10:32; 15:9; Gal 1:13; Phil 3:6); "a change in the nature of Paul's ministry in the later letters rather than a change to pseudonymous authorship probably best accounts for" the increase. (Thielman, l.54 — authorship note, Thielman leans Pauline)
- **[1:22b]** Text/lexical: some read *edōken* ("he gave") as if *ethēken* ("he appointed") → "he made him head." Thielman rejects: standard examples of this meaning "are all debatable"; "far more likely that Paul used the verb in its normal way… God gave Christ to the church." (cites BDAG; Muddiman 2001) (Thielman, ll.56–58)
- **[1:22b]** Thielman's main point: God gave Christ to the church "in Christ's capacity as head over all things." Distinct from 5:23 / Col 1:18 (Christ head OF the church) — here Christ is head over all inimical forces and "serves in this capacity for the benefit of the church" (cf. Col 2:10). (Thielman, l.58)
- **[1:23]** *hētis estin to sōma autou* — Thielman reads *hētis* qualitatively ("which, in truth/in fact") giving "special emphasis… the church is Christ's body: it is indeed his body." (cites Abbott, Eadie, BDAG) (Thielman, l.60)
- **[1:23]** Body-metaphor development traced: 1 Corinthians/Romans (unity exhortation; "we who are many… are one body in Christ"); Colossians (two new moves — church-as-body-of-Christ rises to prominence 1:18, 24; and Christ as HEAD of the church-body 1:18, prompted by the Colossian false teaching that placed Christ alongside other powers, cites Bruce, O'Brien, Murphy-O'Connor). (Thielman, ll.62–68)
- **[1:23]** Two NEW uses of the metaphor in Ephesians: (1) 2:15–16, unity of Jew and Gentile in "one body" = a new human replacing fallen Adam; (2) here at 1:22–23, the head metaphor used "independently to speak of Christ's victorious rule over the inimical powers" — "a direction unique in the Pauline corpus." Because the church is Christ's body and Christ is head over all things, "The church, then, is also in some sense head over all inimical powers, and they lie conquered beneath its feet" (cf. 2:6). (Thielman, ll.72–74)
- **[1:23]** The crux phrase *to plērōma tou ta panta en pasin plēroumenou*. Thielman's rendering: "that which is full of the One who is continuously and completely filled." (Thielman, l.28, l.76) He argues: *plērōma* passive ("that which is full of"), not active (church completing Christ); rejects the ancient "church completes Christ" reading (Origen [Heine 2002], Chrysostom, cf. Calvin) because elsewhere believers are filled/grow (3:19; 4:13; 5:18) while Christ fills (4:10). (Thielman, ll.76–78) *plēroumenou* passive: "the church is that which is filled by the One who is himself filled, presumably Christ" (cites Best, Dawes, Hoehner); present tense = continual filling. (Thielman, l.80) Who fills Christ? Not stated; Colossians helps (fullness of deity dwells in Christ, Col 2:9; 1:19) — "the church is filled by Christ, and Christ himself is filled by God." (Thielman, l.82) *ta panta en pasin* taken adverbially = "entirely," like classical *pantapasi*. (Thielman, l.84) Note: Paul may have prized the p-alliteration (rhetorical device) over clarity. (Thielman, l.86)
- **[1:22, Additional Note]** *kephalē* debate: one side (Mickelsen, Cervin, Perriman) says *kephalē* rarely carried authority/leadership in Greek; other side (Grudem, Fitzmyer) says it did frequently; "source" reading (Bedale). Perriman (1994): term basically meant "most prominent/preeminent"; context decides. Thielman's verdict for 1:22: "the context emphasizes Christ's authority over all things… this must count as an example of the use of *kephalē* to communicate… authority." (Thielman, ll.96–98)

### 2:1–3 (§IV A — Children of Wrath Like All the Rest)
- **[2:1]** Thielman's translation: "And you, when you were dead in your transgressions and sins." *nekrous* ("dead") used metaphorically in Greek for those "morally or spiritually deficient" (cites BDAG, Bultmann TDNT; Epictetus example; Jesus in Matt 8:22; Luke 9:60; John 5:24; the hymn in Eph 5:14). (Thielman, l.152)
- **[2:1]** But when Paul links death with sin (as in Romans) he thinks of "death as the biblical penalty for sin" (Gen 2:16–17; Rom 5:12–14; 6:23; etc.); refers to a present "living death" and to "separation from God both now and in eternity" plus impending eschatological wrath. (Thielman, l.154)
- **[2:1]** *paraptōmata* / *hamartiai* doublet: characteristic Ephesians redundancy (cites Lincoln, Aletti), not a real distinction between "transgressions" and "sins." Rejects the claim (Luz, Pokorný, Hübner) that the plural is "wholly unpauline" as "considerably overstated" (Paul uses plural: 1 Thess 2:16; 1 Cor 15:3,17; Gal 1:4; Rom 4:7; 7:5; 11:27). (Thielman, l.156 — authorship-adjacent defense)
- **[2:2]** Three qualifying phrases on *peripateō* ("walked"). *kata ton aiōna tou kosmou toutou* ("according to the Course of this world"): more than a period of time — "a powerful mode of existence characterized by rebellion against God," personified like sin in Rom 5–8. (cites Schlier, Pokorný, Schwindt) (Thielman, l.162)
- **[2:2]** *kata ton archonta tēs exousias tou aeros* ("Ruler of the realm of the air"). *exousia* = "realm/domain" (used of the devil's realm, Luke 4:6; Col 1:13). *aēr* in Aristotelian cosmology = region below moon/above earth, "habitation of spiritual powers." Cites Plutarch (Mor. 274b: "the open air… full of gods and demons") and Diogenes Laertius on Pythagoras ("all the air is full of souls… called demons"). "the powers that inhabited the air were widely feared." (Thielman, l.164)
- **[2:2]** For Paul the "air" ≈ part of the "heavenly places," location of "every name that is named" (1:21); their Ruler "in Ephesians… could only be 'the devil'" (4:27; 6:11–12). (Thielman, l.166)
- **[2:2]** *tou pneumatos tou nyn energountos en tois hyiois tēs apeitheias* — the "spirit now at work within the sons of disobedience." *apeitheia* connotes not just disobedience but unbelief; "sons of disobedience" = those who have not believed the gospel (1:13) and stand under God's wrath. (Thielman, l.168)
- **[2:3]** *kai hēmeis pantes* — Thielman REJECTS the "vast company" reading that this means "we Jews also" (contra a broadening to include Jews): "in Ephesians ethnicity does not enter the argument until 2:11." First-person plural = Paul + his readers (all Christians), showing the plight "affected every Christian, without exception, himself included." (Thielman, l.172) [Contrast: this is Thielman diverging from the majority reading.]
- **[2:3]** Plight covers the entire person — *epithymiai* ("cravings") of flesh, *thelēmata* ("desires") of flesh, and desires of *dianoiai* ("thoughts"). *epithymia* usually negative in Paul; *thelēma* neutral but here negative, possibly hinting sexual desire (Schrenk TDNT); *dianoiai* = mental processes here with negative connotation ("mind of the flesh… at enmity with God," Rom 8:7). (Thielman, ll.174–180)
- **[2:3]** Flesh called "ours" and neutral terms used → Paul "thinks of neither the flesh nor the mind as outside powers that have driven people, against their will"; "All humankind has chosen willfully and thoughtfully to live among the sons of disobedience." (Thielman, l.184)
- **[2:3]** *tekna physei orgēs* ("children of wrath by nature"). *orgēs* = "genitive of destination" (destiny of wrath); *physei* ("by nature") = "the condition into which someone was born… by birth." Emphasizes that though culpable, humans "have chosen this path inevitably, in agreement with the state into which they were born." (cf. Rom 5:12) (Thielman, ll.186–188)
- **[2:2, Additional Note]** *aiōn* ambiguity: could mean "age" (temporal) or personal being. Thielman rejects (as based on "evidence of uncertain historical worth," cites Nock, Fraser, Drijvers) the theory of a god Aiōn worshiped ~200 BC in Egypt; but notes by the 2nd c. AD "Aion was in the air" (coins, gnosticism [Irenaeus, Hippolytus], magical papyri; Ignatius Eph 19.2; Epictetus). Verdict: "a firm decision… does not seem possible"; best (with Schwindt 2002) that *aiōn* and *kosmos* overlap to describe "a powerful sphere of existence that is opposed to God." (Thielman, ll.198–208)
- **[2:2, Additional Note]** *tou pneumatos* — several construals surveyed; Thielman's preferred: syntactically parallel to *tēs exousias*, dependent on *ton archonta*; refers to an evil "spirit" pervading the devil's realm and at work in the disobedient, forming "an antithetical parallel to God himself, who 'effected' (*enērgēsen*)" the resurrection (1:20). (Thielman, ll.210–216)

### 2:4–7 (§IV B — Objects of God's Mercy)
- **[2:4–7]** Two emphases: (1) God's response arises from "his persistently merciful, loving, and gracious character" — "rich" mercy, "great" love, "surpassing wealth" of grace; (2) "the critical role of Christ." A "studied parallel" between God raising/seating Christ (1:19–21) and God making believers alive/raising/seating them. Careful qualification: "Paul is careful not to say that believers have been exalted to God's right hand (cf. 2:6 with 1:20)." (Thielman, ll.235–239)
- **[2:4]** *ho de theos* ("but God"). Participle *ōn* ("because he is [rich in mercy]") parallel to *dia tēn pollēn agapēn autou*; both give the cause. (Thielman, l.247)
- **[2:4]** Echoes OT/Jewish/Christian theme: LORD "abounding in steadfast love" (*rab-ḥesed*), rendered *polyeleos* in LXX, usually in contexts where God could justly pour out wrath (Jonah 4:2 re Nineveh). Phrase entered Jewish liturgy — the "Thirteen Attributes of God" (Exod 34:6–7), still in synagogue use (cites Sarna 1991). Cf. Matt 18:33 parable. (Thielman, l.249)
- **[2:4]** Love (*agapē*) major theme in Ephesians; cognate accusative "the love with which he loved" emphasizes it. (Thielman, l.251)
- **[2:5–6]** Three *syn*- verbs: *synezōopoiēsen* (made alive together with — appears only here and Col 2:13 in all Greek prior to Paul), *synēgeiren* (raised together with — only here + Col 2:12; 3:1 in NT), *synekathisen* (seated together with — only transitive NT use here). "The most unusual element… is their past tense": the believer's life, resurrection, and enthronement "are events that have already happened." (Thielman, l.257)
- **[2:5b]** *chariti este sesōsmenoi* ("by grace you are saved"), interjected. *charis* emphasizes "the absolutely free nature of God's action." Roman-context note: *charis* commonly described the "massively generous benefactions of the Julio-Claudian emperors" (cites Harrison 1999/2003); Paul may imply God's benefaction "outstripped anything Rome had to offer" (cites Whitlark 2003). (Thielman, l.259)
- **[2:5]** *este sesōsmenoi* = perfect periphrastic → present state: "Paul's readers are saved." In undisputed letters Paul normally speaks of salvation as future; "the use of the perfect tense in Eph. 2:5 and 8 for salvation is unusual… salvation is something that is emphatically present." (Thielman, ll.261–265)
- **[2:5–6]** Note: "there is no mention of Christ's cross here, but only of his resurrection and victorious exaltation" — stands out vs Rom 5:6–11 and Col 2:11–15. (Thielman, l.267)
- **[2:5–6, authorship excursus]** Position: some (Luz, Hahn, Berger) read the realized-eschatology emphasis and cross-absence as evidence of pseudonymous, second-generation Christianity where cross/Spirit/apocalyptic faded. Thielman's response: if Ephesians is Paul's, "we need imagine nothing more than a shift of emphasis… to address a particular pastoral situation" — readers "tempted… to fear the rulers and authorities… and to placate them" (cites Arnold 1989). Also: Ephesians isn't devoid of suffering-with-Christ (3:1, 13; 6:20), and undisputed letters come close to realized language (2 Cor 4:10–12; Rom 8:10; Phil 3:20; Gal 2:20). Conclusion: Ephesians "does not stand in contradiction to the theology of the undisputed letters but places emphasis on one side." (Thielman, ll.271–277 — Thielman defends Pauline authorship)
- **[2:7]** Purpose: *hina endeixētai* — God saved them "so that… he might show… the surpassing wealth of his grace." *hyperballon* echoes imperial-benefaction inscriptions (Harrison, Whitlark). Three phrases: *en tois aiōsin tois eperchomenois* ("in the coming ages" = duration, all future ages — rejects "attacking Aeons" personal reading), *en chrēstotēti* ("by kindness"), *en Christō Iēsou* ("in Christ Jesus" = sphere). (Thielman, ll.279–289)

### 2:8–10 (§IV C — The Nature and Consequences of God's Grace)
- **[2:8–10]** Salvation "entirely at God's initiative and as a free gift" — vocabulary: *charis* ("grace"), *dōron* ("gift"), received *dia pisteōs* ("through faith") meaning "no meritorious human effort," and even good works God "prepared beforehand" (*proētoimasen*). Syntax fronts "grace," "God," and "his" for emphasis. (Thielman, ll.322–324)
- **[2:8a]** Thielman's translation: "For by that grace you are saved, through faith; and this is not from yourselves; it is God's gift, not from works, so that no one might boast." (Thielman, l.338) Article before *chariti* points back to "that grace" of 2:5, 7 (cites Wallace). (Thielman, l.342)
- **[2:8a]** *dia pisteōs*: faith is the human "response"; they must "receive" salvation (Rom 5:17), trusting the gospel (1:13). (Thielman, l.344)
- **[2:8a]** Thielman REJECTS Theodoret's reading that the readers "had only faith to offer, but divine grace worked with it": "In Paul's thinking, faith is not something that people offer to God and with which God's grace then cooperates." Faith is "aligned with grace," both opposed to human offering; "To say that salvation comes 'through faith'… is to further enhance the notion that it arises from the grace of God." (cites Haupt) (Thielman, l.346) [Attributed rejection of a patristic view.]
- **[2:8b–9]** *touto* ("this") = the salvation just described, not from *ex hymōn* ("from yourselves"); had to come as God's *dōron*. *hina mē tis kauchēsētai* ("so that no one might boast") = "an allusive way of saying, 'so that all might boast in God alone'"; parallels Rom 4–5 boasting theme. (Thielman, ll.348–350)
- **[2:8–9, authorship note]** Difference from Rom 4–5: no verb "justify," and no "works of the [Jewish] law" context. Position (Luz, Lincoln): shows Ephesians postdates resolved Jew/Gentile tension and faded apocalyptic. Thielman's counter: undisputed Paul can exclude boasting apart from Judaizing struggle (1 Cor 1:26–30; 4:7); Eph 6:10–17 still assumes present struggle with "world rulers of this darkness." "the thought of Eph. 2:8–9 is Pauline"; precedent for redefining "works" as human effort generally in Rom 4:1–8. (Thielman, ll.352–356 — Thielman defends Pauline authorship)
- **[2:10]** *poiēma* ("handiwork/creation") — only other Pauline/NT use is Rom 1:20 (works of God at creation). Fronted *autou* ("his") emphatic. New-creation idea in Gal 6:15; 2 Cor 5:17; Col 3:10; here Christ is agent of the new creation (2:15b). (Thielman, ll.360–362)
- **[2:10]** *epi ergois agathois* ("for good works"). Note on "un-Pauline" plural "good works" (appears elsewhere in Pauline corpus only in the disputed Pastorals) — counterbalanced by the *epi*+dative purpose idiom (all 3 NT uses Pauline). Good works are "neither the basis of salvation nor… given equal status with faith" (rejects F.C. Baur's view that a post-Pauline writer more like James did this). *ktisthentes* (aorist) shows works are consequence of an accomplished new creation. (Thielman, ll.364–368)
- **[2:10]** *proētoimasen* ("prepared beforehand"): God planned the works "since the beginning of the world" (cf. Wis 9:8; Philo Creation 77; Rom 9:23; Josephus Ant. 17.121 for the term). Even in good works believers "have nothing to boast about." Closes 2:1–10 by contrasting the old "walk" (2:2) with the new. (Thielman, l.370)

### 2:11–13 (§V A — Special Plight of the Gentiles and God's Response)
- **[2:11–13, framing]** 2:11–22 shows how God's power affects believers "as a people"; roughly parallels 2:1–10 (plight → response → present result) but is HORIZONTAL where 2:1–10 was VERTICAL. 2:1–10 = individual, Christ's resurrection/ascension; 2:11–22 = social alienation Israel/Gentiles, Christ's DEATH as solution "which set aside the Mosaic law, with its tendency to divide Jews from Gentiles." "By overcoming the hostility between God and all human beings, Christ's death breaks down the wall of hostility between Jews and Gentiles." (Thielman, ll.395–399)
- **[2:11–13]** *syn*- compounds shift from vertical (2:5–6: *synezōopoiēsen*, *synēgeiren*, *synekathisen*) to horizontal (2:19–22: *sympolitai*, *synarmologoumenē*, *synoikodomeisthe*). (Thielman, ll.401–433)
- **[2:11]** Thielman's translation: "once you Gentiles in the flesh—those called 'foreskin' by the so-called circumcision (done by hand in the flesh)." *dio* draws inference from all 2:1–10. *mnēmoneuete* = "continue to remember." (Thielman, ll.484–486)
- **[2:11]** *akrobystia* ("foreskin") echoes LXX Gen 17:11–12; *legomenoi* ("called") "hints that *akrobystia* was used derisively." (Thielman, l.490)
- **[2:11]** *hē legomenē peritomē* ("the so-called circumcision"): two readings (neutral self-designation [Best, Muddiman] vs negative "not really circumcised since true circumcision is spiritual" [Ellicott, Abbott, Eadie; Rom 2:28–29]). Since Paul next uses *cheiropoiētos* ("done by hand") negatively, "he probably also intends… *legomenē* negatively." Real circumcision "not done by hand" (Col 2:11–12), involves Christ's death; physical circumcision no longer "necessary for membership in God's people." (Thielman, ll.492–494)
- **[2:11]** Thielman's explanation for the "note of distance between Christians and Jews": historical presuppositions — before the gospel Jews had "enormous religious advantages," but after the gospel these "were overshadowed by the rejection of the gospel among most Jews." Israel, historically "near," "nevertheless needs to be reconciled to him through faith." (Thielman, l.496)
- **[2:12]** Thielman's translation: "at that time, outside Christ, alienated from Israel's way of life and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world." Five Gentile disadvantages, four tied to lack of access to Scriptures. (Thielman, ll.484, 498)
  1. *chōris christou* ("outside Christ") — most important, heads the list; the promise of the Messiah in Israel's Scriptures (Rom 9:5; Gal 3:16, 29). (Thielman, ll.500–502)
  2. *apēllotriōmenoi tēs politeias tou Israēl* ("alienated from Israel's way of life"). *politeia* — three traditional meanings: (a) "way of life" of the Jewish people (Origen and Jerome held this; modern commentators "curiously neglected this option"); (b) "citizenship"/special rights; (c) "commonwealth"/political body. Thielman: don't distinguish too sharply — cites Cohen 1999, and Josephus Ant. 15.254 (Hyrcanus "altered their way of life [*politeia*]" of the Idumeans). (Thielman, ll.504–508)
  3. *xenoi tōn diathēkōn tēs epangelias* ("strangers to the covenants of promise") — probably the Abrahamic covenant and the new covenant (Mosaic covenant is contrasted/passed away, Gal 3:17–18; 2 Cor 3:7–11; Rom 7:6). "Promise" = possibly the Spirit (Gal 3:14; Eph 1:13) and/or the Messiah. (Thielman, ll.510–514)
  4. "no hope" — present participle *echontes*: constant hopelessness; not felt despair (Best) but from a Christian retrospective, "their future held only 'the wrath of God.'" (Thielman, l.516)
  5. *atheoi en tō kosmō* ("without God in the world"). *atheos* was a Gentile slander against Jews (Josephus Ag. Ap. 2.148) and later Christians (Justin, Athenagoras, Mart. Pol.). Polycarp turned the slogan "Away with the atheists" back on the pagans (Mart. Pol. 9.2). (Thielman, l.518)
- **[2:13]** Thielman's translation: "But now, in Christ Jesus, you who were once far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ." *nuni de* Pauline hinge marking dramatic change. Language from Isa 57:19 ("Peace, peace, to the far and the near") — *makran* / *engys*; Isaiah's wider context emphasizes "the unification of Israel with all peoples in the worship of God" (Isa 55:5; 56:6–8; cites Moritz 1996a). Inclusion happened *en Christō Iēsou* and *en tō haimati tou Christou* ("by the blood of Christ"). (Thielman, ll.524–528)
- **[2:11, Additional Notes]** *cheiropoiētos* ("done by hand"): in LXX always negative (handmade idols); in NT (apart from Eph 2:11) always of the temple, negatively (Mark 14:58; Acts 7:48; Heb 9:11, 24). Weighs against Yee (2005) that the term isn't negative here; means physical circumcision "is no longer the critical boundary marker." Circumcision as social distinction / pejorative (m. Ned. 3.11; Martial "circumcised poet"; Philo Spec. Laws 1.1 "object of ridicule"). (Thielman, ll.538–544)

### 2:14–18 (§V B — Christ Is the Believing Community's Peace)
- **[2:14–18, intro]** Discrete unit: begins with emphatic *autos*, shifts to first-person plural, uses active-voice participles for Christ's action — "Christ's own actions rather than God's action through Christ… take the spotlight." Syntax "extraordinarily difficult"; mingles "the unification of Jews and Gentiles and the reconciliation of humanity with God." (Thielman, l.561)
- **[2:14–18]** THREE explanatory approaches surveyed and all judged too uncertain to control exegesis: (1) Jewish-Christian midrash on Isa 9:6–7; 52:7; 57:19 linked by catchword "peace" (Stuhlmacher, Schnackenburg); (2) an encomium/eulogy on Christ using rhetorical amplification (*auxēsis*) — epideictic (Faust, Aletti, Yee); (3) MOST POPULAR: a pre-existing hymn (originally about Christ breaking the wall separating heaven from earth, Hellenistic-Jewish/gnostic cosmology) modified by the author to refer to the Mosaic-law wall dividing Jews/Gentiles (Schlier, Gnilka, Lincoln, Pokorný). Thielman's verdict: the hymn theory is "too uncertain to contribute to a reliable interpretive strategy" — Ephesians is generally syntactically difficult and ~10% of its vocabulary is NT-unique anyway (cites Best). (Thielman, ll.563–571)
- **[2:14–18]** Thielman reads it as a Pauline excursus (like 1 Cor 13; 2 Cor 2:14–7:1). Summary thesis: "By his death on the cross, Christ tore down and set aside the Mosaic law. It had formed a wall of hostility that divided Jews from Gentiles and… blocked the way between humanity and God." Assumes the Romans theology of the law (Rom 5:20; 7:11–12). (Thielman, l.575)
- **[2:14–15a]** Thielman's translation: "For he himself is our peace, who made both things one and tore down in his flesh the middle wall, that is, the fence—the enmity—by setting aside the law of commandments [promulgated] in [the form of] decrees." (Thielman, l.581)
- **[2:14]** *estin hē eirēnē hēmōn* ("is our peace") — those "in Christ" assume Christ's qualities; Christ is undivided so those identified with him are at peace with one another. "Peace" is Hebraic *šālôm* but here esp. "the 'opposite of war'" given the Jew/Gentile alienation focus. (Thielman, l.585)
- **[2:14]** *ho poiēsas ta amphotera hen* ("who made both things one") — odd NEUTER *ta amphotera*/*hen* (vs masculine in 2:16, 18). Some read it as "undigested bits of traditional material" about heaven/earth spheres (Schlier, Gnilka, Lincoln); Thielman prefers Best's suggestion: spatial imagery of a Jewish "region" and Gentile "region" (*chōrion*, neuter) separated by the wall. (Thielman, l.587)
- **[2:14 — MIDDLE WALL, see dedicated section below]**
- **[2:14]** *tēn echthran* ("the enmity") — syntactically ambiguous (object of *lysas* "tore down" or of *katargēsas* "set aside"). Thielman: "slightly more likely that *tēn echthran* goes with *lysas*" (closer, an afterthought). So: "the middle wall, that is, the fence—the enmity." (Thielman, ll.603–605)
- **[2:14]** *en tē sarki autou* ("in his flesh") — Thielman: modifies *lysas* (first option): "the middle wall was torn down in Christ's flesh" (favored by Greek-native Fathers Origen, Theodoret, Oecumenius; and echoed by *tēn echthran en autō* in 2:16). Refers to Christ's DEATH on the cross, not the incarnation (contra Calvin); a physical sacrifice involving "blood" and "flesh." (Thielman, ll.607–619)
- **[2:15a — LAW, see dedicated section below]**
- **[2:15b]** Thielman's translation: "in order that he might create the two into one new human being in him, so making peace." (Thielman, l.581)
- **[2:15b — ONE NEW HUMAN BEING, see dedicated section below]**
- **[2:16]** *apokatallaxē* ("he might reconcile"). Reconciliation is distinctively Pauline (2 Cor 5:18–20; Rom 5:10–11). Three distinctions in Col/Eph: (1) compound *apokatallassō* (intensifies, doesn't change meaning); (2) Christ, not God, is reconciler; (3) in Colossians God reconciles the whole cosmos (*ta panta*) whereas here God reconciles people. (Thielman, ll.639–641)
- **[2:16]** *tous amphoterous* (masculine "both") reconciled to God. Change from neuter (2:14) explained simply: *kainos anthrōpos* (masculine) was introduced at 2:15b. Even Jews (nearer to God, 2:12) "were still in need of reconciliation." (Thielman, l.643)
- **[2:16]** *en heni sōmati* ("in one body") = NOT the crucified body of Christ but the "one new human being" of 2:15 = the church, unified across ethnic lines. (Thielman, l.645)
- **[2:16]** *dia tou staurou* ("through the cross"); *apokteinas tēn echthran* ("by killing the enmity"). Here *echthra* = enmity between GOD and rebellious humanity (not Jew/Gentile as in 2:14), given the reconciliation-to-God theme; cf. Rom 5:10. *en autō* ("in it") = the cross. Reminiscent of Col 2:14–15 (nailing decrees to the cross, triumphing over rulers). (Thielman, ll.647–651)
- **[2:16]** Thielman's synthesis: "The Mosaic law was as tightly bound to the enmity between God and all humanity as it was to the enmity between Jews and Gentiles." Its holy decrees, meeting a humanity under the world/devil/flesh, "served only to reveal the depth of humanity's rebellion"; Christ's death set it aside, creating a new people AND removing "the case against all humanity codified in the Mosaic law." (Thielman, l.651)
- **[2:17]** "And he came and preached peace to you who were far and peace to those who were near." Allusion to Isa 52:7a and 57:19. Peter already connected Isa 52:7 with Christ (Acts 10:36). Paul "cleverly restructures" Isa 57:19 so one "peace" goes with "far" and one with "near," emphasizing "the evenhandedness of the proclamation" — here "peace" = between both groups and God (not Jew/Gentile as in vv.14–15). (Thielman, ll.653–655)
- **[2:18]** "for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father." *hoti* indicates "the basis for, or proof of, the peace." *prosagōgē* ("access") — could mean access to a king (Xenophon, Cyrus example, cites Fee), but since God is depicted as Father, Thielman prefers the cognate verb *prosagō*'s sense of "bringing offerings, prayers, or people before God" (cites Gärtner, Lincoln): Christ removed the Mosaic-law barrier and "so provided access to God… just as a priest might bring an offering to a deity." *di' autou* = Christ's death. (Thielman, ll.657–661)
- **[2:18]** *en heni pneumati* = "united together in one Spirit," NOT "by means of one Spirit" (means of access = Christ's death already stated; "one" used for Jew/Gentile unity in 2:15, 16). (Thielman, l.663)

### 2:19–22 (§V C — Gentile Christians as an Integral Part of God's Household)
- **[2:19–22, framing]** Progressive imagery: "household," "building," "dwelling place." Six *-oik-* words; reaches back to *oikonomia* (1:10) and forward (3:2, 9). Paul may think of the universe as a household God administers as Father. (Thielman, ll.449–451, 694–704)
- **[2:19]** Thielman's translation: "So then, you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens together with the saints and members of God's household." *ara oun* signals tight logical connection. Four social/political terms: *xenoi* ("strangers"), *paroikoi* ("aliens"/resident aliens), *sympolitai* ("citizens together"), *oikeioi* ("members of the household"). Ancient city lists ranked *politai* > *paroikoi*/*katoikoi* > *xenoi* (cites Philo Posterity 109). Paul uses them "metaphorically and loosely," painting "in broad brush strokes." (Thielman, ll.712–716)
- **[2:19]** *hagioi* ("saints") = believers without ethnic distinction. Thielman REJECTS readings that Gentiles are now citizens with Israel (Barth), or with Jewish Christians (E. Scott, Dibelius, Faust, Sellin), or with angels (Schlier, Gnilka): "Rather, they form one citizenry with all other believers" (cites Lincoln, Aletti, Hoehner). (Thielman, l.718)
- **[2:20]** Thielman's translation: "because you were built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the most important stone." *epoikodomēthentes* (aorist) points back to the readers' response to the gospel (1:13). (Thielman, l.720)
- **[2:20]** Foundation = *hoi apostoloi kai prophētai* ("the apostles and prophets"), bound by a single article but NOT the same people (Paul distinguishes them in 4:11; 1 Cor 12:28). *apostoloi* = those who first took the gospel to Gentiles (Barnabas, Timothy, Silvanus, Apollos, preeminently Paul). *prophētai* = NOT OT prophets but NT prophets (as in 3:5; 4:11; 1 Cor 12:28) who directed the church's outward movement to Gentiles (Acts 13:1–3; 15:32). (Thielman, ll.724–726)
- **[2:20 — AKROGŌNIAIOS, see Temple section below]**
- **[2:21]** Thielman's translation: "in whom the whole building, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord." (Thielman, l.710)
- **[2:22]** Thielman's translation: "in whom also you are being built together into the dwelling place of God in the Spirit." (Thielman, l.710)
- **[2:19, house imagery]** *oikeioi tou theou* (members of God's household, v.19) links to *katoikētērion tou theou* (house of God, v.22): "the place where God lives, by his Spirit, with his people." (Thielman, l.760)

---

## Middle wall (2:14) — full detail

Thielman's translation of the phrase: "he... tore down in his flesh the middle wall, that is, the fence—the enmity" (*to mesotoichon tou phragmou*). (l.581, l.589)

**Lexical data:**
- *mesotoichon* ("middle wall") is rare; where it occurs it refers to "an outside wall or to a partition wall in a house or temple." Josephus uses the related *ton meson toichon* for the wall separating the holy of holies from the rest of Solomon's temple (Ant. 8.71; cf. 1 Kings 6:16–17; BDAG 635). (Thielman, l.589)
- *phragmos* (explanatory/epexegetical genitive): "a 'fence' or 'hedge' that encloses something, shutting it off and protecting it" (Isa 5:2, 5; Sir 36:25; Mark 12:1; Matt 21:33); appears only here in the Pauline corpus. "Christ, then, tore down a partition that was also an enclosing fence." (Thielman, l.589)

**Four interpretive options surveyed:**
1. **Herod's temple balustrade** — the short stone wall/*dryphaktos* separating the Gentile court from the inner sections (Josephus Ant. 15.417; J.W. 5.193–95). Idea is "very old, going back at least to Anselm of Laon" (early 12th c.); supporters Abbott, Robinson, MacDonald. Thielman's OBJECTION: "It is unlikely… Paul would have expected a wide audience of Gentiles in Asia Minor to understand an allusive reference to a specific feature of the Jerusalem temple's exterior architecture." (Thielman, l.591)
2. **Hymn/tradition about heaven–earth separation** — *mesotoichon* from a hymn (Hellenistic-Jewish/gnostic cosmology), later glossed with *phragmos* to suit the Mosaic law's protective function (Gnilka, Lincoln, Pokorný). Thielman's OBJECTION: same as the general hymn-theory objection; also, "it is difficult to see why, if the term *mesotoichon* seemed inadequate to Paul, he did not simply replace it with *phragmos* rather than adding *phragmos* to it." (Thielman, ll.593–595)
3. **Non-specific social separation** — the wall symbolizes social boundaries generally, no specific institution (Best, Yee). (Thielman, l.597)
4. **THIELMAN'S OWN VIEW: the middle wall = the Mosaic/Jewish law.** Argument: We shouldn't exaggerate Judaism's strangeness — Cohen (1999: 28): "Not a single ancient author says that Jews are distinctive because of their looks, clothing, speech, names, or occupations"; diaspora Jews "were not easily recognizable." The most reliable indicator of Jewishness "was observance of the Jewish law" (Cohen). Ephesian Jews (49–48 BC, Lucius Lentulus Crus exemption) were distinguished because they "observed" and "practiced" Jewish rites (*hiera Ioudaika*) = kept the law (Josephus Ant. 14.228 etc.). **KEY PARALLEL — Letter of Aristeas 139:** the law was compared to "iron walls" (*sidēra teichē*) that God used to "enclose" Israel "with a fence" (*periphrassō*) to keep them from mixing with "other nations" (*alla ethnē*). Thielman's conclusion: "it seems most likely that by the phrase *to mesotoichon tou phragmou* Paul meant the Jewish law. The Jewish law was both a 'partition' that separated Jews from Gentiles and a 'fence' that enclosed the Jewish people, keeping them safe from Gentile influences." (Thielman, ll.599–601)

**Summary restatement (l.671):** "Christ tore down the Mosaic law as both a 'partition' separating Jews from Gentiles and as a 'fence' enclosing the Jewish people and keeping them safe from Gentile influences."

---

## The law of commandments in decrees (2:15a) — full detail
Thielman's rendering: "by setting aside the law of commandments [promulgated] in [the form of] decrees" (*ho nomos tōn entolōn en dogmasin*, set aside by *katargēsas*). (Thielman, l.581, ll.621–633)
- *katargēsas* ("setting aside") — Paul uses the same verb (passive) in 2 Cor 3:7–14 for the Mosaic era being "set aside," and Rom 7:2, 6 for believers "released" from the law. Active voice + "tore down"/"kill" gives "a somewhat stronger connotation." (Thielman, l.621)
- Tension with undisputed Paul (Rom 3:31: gospel does NOT set aside the law; ongoing ethical use Gal 5:14; Rom 13:8–10). Position (Lincoln, Schnackenburg, MacDonald): the contradiction is real and marks a post-Pauline author for whom the law = past salvation history; the redundant phrase "emphasizes the completeness of the law's abrogation." (Thielman, l.625)
- Alternative narrowing readings REJECTED by Thielman: Calvin — only "ceremonies" abolished, moral law remains; others — only the "commanding character." (Thielman, l.627)
- **Thielman's own view:** *tōn entolōn* = content of the law; *en dogmasin* = "the method of the commandments' promulgation" (decrees). "Paul clearly intends the phrase to refer to the entire Mosaic law." Redundancy is characteristic Ephesians style. (Thielman, l.629) BUT Christ did not set aside the need for commandments in Christianity (Paul cites Decalogue command in Eph 6:2–3); rather, believers obeying such parts obey them "not… as the Mosaic law." The Mosaic law "governed Israel for a specific period of time" (Gal 3:19), reached "its divinely appointed end" (2 Cor 3:13; Rom 10:4); the new people's law = "the law of Christ" (Gal 6:2). The Mosaic law remains "authoritative Scripture within the new people of God, but in a different way," its commandments passing "through the filter of the gospel." (Thielman, l.631)
- What Christ removed = "the hostile purposes to which human sinfulness had often put the Mosaic law's good, but temporary, commands about separating from the Gentiles" — "This toxic mixture of the law and human sinfulness" (Rom 5:20; 7:5–25) led Paul to speak of the law in negative terms here. (Thielman, l.633)

---

## One new human being (2:15) — full detail
Thielman's rendering: "in order that he might create the two into one new human being in him" (*heis kainos anthrōpos*, verb *ktizō* → *ktisē*). (Thielman, l.581, l.637)
- *ktizō* ("create"): Paul already used it of the individual believer as God's new creation (2:10); "Here too Paul has the new creation in mind, but now conceived as a CORPORATE event, making peace between the two estranged groups." (Thielman, l.637)
- By union with Christ, believers become united with one another across the former social barriers, and "so, like Christ himself, become a new Adam (cf. 1 Cor. 15:22, 45–49; Col. 3:10–11; Lincoln 1990)." (Thielman, l.637) [This is the Adam/new-humanity typology — the "one new human being" = a new Adam replacing the fallen Adam; cross-ref 1:23 note at l.72: the "one body" of 2:15–16 "is a new human that replaces the fallen Adam."]
- *poiōn* ("making [peace]") = "a textbook example of an adverbial participle of result" (present tense, follows the verb; cites Wallace). "So the result of this newly created man… is peace between formerly hostile Jews and Gentiles." (Thielman, l.637)
- *en autō* ("in him[self]"): the creation of the new humanity happens in Christ. (Thielman, l.637)
- Purpose structure (2:15b–16): Christ set aside the law for TWO purposes — (1) *ktisē* create one new human being (→ peace between Jew/Gentile); (2) *apokatallaxē* reconcile both to God. (Thielman, l.635)

---

## Temple / naos (2:19–22) — full detail

**Foundation and cornerstone (2:20):**
- *akrogōniaios* ("most important stone") applied to Christ Jesus, intensified by *autou* ("himself"), setting Christ apart from apostles/prophets as "the most important element in the building." (Thielman, l.728)
- The term is rare — surfaces only in Isa 28:16 LXX, then until the mid-2nd c. only in Christian tradition dependent on it (1 Pet 2:6; Barn. 6.2–3; Justin Dial. 114.4; 126.1). Etymology: *akron* ("topmost/outermost/inmost") + *gōniaios* ("at the angle") — could be a stone crowning the building (added last) OR a foundation stone at the most distant corner (placed first). (Thielman, ll.728–730)
- **Two positions:**
  - "Capstone/keystone added last" (Jeremias, Dibelius, Gnilka; Lincoln, Aletti): supported by Symmachus (2 Kings 25:17; Ps 118:22) and T. Sol. 22.6–23.4 (elevated stone placed last in the temple); and by the parallel of 4:13–16 where the church grows UP to Christ the head. (Thielman, ll.732–734)
  - "Foundation stone set low, giving guidance/stability" (McKelvey, Schnackenburg, Sellin): consistent with the present-tense verbs (building under construction); consistent with Isa 28:16 (near *themelios*, "foundation") and 1 Cor 3:11 (Christ = *themelios*). (Thielman, ll.736–738)
  - Best (1998): "in the present state of our knowledge the problem is insoluble." (Thielman, l.740)
- **Thielman's own resolution:** the problem may come from "too wooden an understanding of the metaphor." Following Mayer (2002): Christ as cornerstone is "at the same time *fundamentum fundamentorum* and *finis finium*" — "the 'topmost foundation stone,'" both anchoring/guiding the church's growth (Isa 28:16 Zion foundation) and encompassing his role as "head over all things" (1:22–23) and the head toward which the body grows (4:13, 15–16). (Thielman, l.742)

**The building growing into a temple (2:21):**
- Thielman renders "the whole building" (*pasa oikodomē*); rejects "every building" (contra Lightfoot) because the figure assumes a single building. Additional note: some scribes added the article *hē*; correct reading is *pasa oikodomē* without article, which can and here must mean "the whole building." (Thielman, ll.746, 772)
- *synarmologoumenē* ("being joined together") appears only here and 4:16 in all known Greek prior to 2nd c. AD — "Clearly Paul coined it to match his other *syn-* words in chapter 2." Base *harmologeō* = architectural "fit together/join" (cites P.Ryl. 233.6). Readers are "part of a building in the process of growing by being tightly fitted together 'with' (*syn-*) other believers across ethnic boundary lines." (Thielman, l.748)
- *naos hagios en kyriō* ("a holy temple in the Lord"): Paul "was probably thinking specifically of the Jewish temple" and its role in Israel's restoration. Prepared by the Isa 28:16 allusion (cornerstone in Zion). Isa 56:3–8 refers to inclusion of the nations in temple worship during Israel's restoration; Paul's Isa 57:19 allusions (2:13, 17) confirm this Isaianic frame (cites McKelvey, Beale). *en kyriō* = "the Lord Jesus Christ" (not the Father): the temple's location "is in the sphere defined by Jesus Christ… a multiethnic temple, the fulfillment of Jewish eschatological expectations… not a physical building." (Thielman, ll.750–754)

**The dwelling place (2:22):**
- *en hō kai hymeis* ("in whom also you") — Paul turns directly to his readers (as in 1:13). *synoikodomeisthe* ("being built together," present tense, *syn-* prefix) — joined "together with" other believers, "specifically other Jewish believers since the destruction of the dividing wall of hostility (2:14)." (Thielman, l.756)
- *katoikētērion tou theou en pneumati* ("the dwelling place of God in the Spirit"). *katoikētērion* — in LXX often for dwellings of people/animals, but sometimes God's dwelling in heaven (1 Kings 8:39) or in Zion's sanctuary (Exod 15:17; Ps 76:2). Paul chose it "because of its biblical associations with God's temple"; like *naos*, refers to the temple of eschatologically restored Israel. *en pneumati* tells "how God dwells within this building: he does so 'in' or 'by' the Spirit." (Thielman, l.758)
- Brings the imagery "full circle": household of God (*oikeioi*, v.19) = house of God (*katoikētērion*, v.22). (Thielman, l.760)

## Named scholars / positions cited (selected)
- **Ancient/patristic:** Origen (Heine 2002 — favored "in his flesh" modifying *lysas*; church-completes-Christ reading of *plērōma* rejected by Thielman), Chrysostom (church completes Christ), Theodoret (R. Hill 2001 — "collection of the faithful" gloss; faith-cooperates-with-grace reading of 2:8, REJECTED by Thielman; favored "in his flesh"→*lysas*), Jerome (*politeia* = "way of life"; on *atheoi*), Oecumenius, Calvin (rejected on "in his flesh"=incarnation and on the ceremonial-law narrowing of 2:15), Anselm of Laon (temple-balustrade reading of the wall).
- **Ancient sources quoted as data:** Josephus (Ant. 8.71 middle wall of temple; Ant. 15.417 / J.W. 5.193–95 temple balustrade; Ant. 14.228+ Ephesian Jews' exemption; Ant. 15.254 Hyrcanus/*politeia*; Ant. 17.121 *proētoimazō*), **Letter of Aristeas 139** (law as "iron walls"/"fence" enclosing Israel — the key parallel for the middle wall), Philo (Posterity 109 social speech; Spec. Laws 1.1 circumcision ridiculed; Creation 77; Planting 47), Plutarch (Mor. 274b air full of gods/demons), Diogenes Laertius (8.32 Pythagoras, air full of souls/demons), Epictetus/Arrian, Ignatius (Eph 19.2 aeons), Mart. Pol. 9.2 (Polycarp "away with the atheists"), Martial (Epig. — "circumcised poet"), Cohen 1999 (Jews not readily recognizable; law-observance the marker), T. Sol. 22.6–23.4 (elevated cornerstone), Symmachus (elevated stone).
- **Modern:** Lincoln (frequent — 2:5 central; hymn theory; post-Pauline readings, often contested by Thielman), Best (1998 — "region" suggestion on *ta amphotera*; wall = general social separation; cornerstone "insoluble"; Ephesians vocabulary stats), O'Brien, Hoehner, Schnackenburg, Gnilka, Pokorný (hymn theory), Schlier (hymn/heaven-earth wall), Arnold 1989/1995 (magic/powers; pastoral situation), Stuhlmacher (midrash), Faust/Aletti/Yee (encomium; Yee on *cheiropoiētos* and the wall, both contested), McKelvey (foundation-stone cornerstone; temple/Isaiah), Beale 2004 (temple), Mayer 2002 (*fundamentum/finis* cornerstone resolution), Moritz 1996a (Ps 110; Isa 57:19), Hay 1973, Harrison 1999/2003 & Whitlark 2003 (imperial-benefaction *charis*/*hyperballō* background), Schwindt 2002 (*aiōn*/*kosmos* overlap), Luz (post-Pauline apocalyptic-fading thesis, contested), F.C. Baur (works=faith, rejected), Wallace (grammar), Grudem/Fitzmyer vs Mickelsen/Cervin/Perriman (*kephalē* debate).

## Notable Greek terms with glosses (as given by Thielman)
- *energeia* / *enērgēsen* — "effect" / "he effected" (1:19–20)
- *hyperanō* — "high above" (1:21)
- *en tois epouraniois* — "in the heavenly places" (1:20)
- *archē, exousia, dynamis, kyriotēs* — rule, authority, power, lordship (1:21)
- *ekklēsia* — "church"/assembly (1:22); *syllogos* (Theodoret) — "collection"
- *kephalē* — "head" (1:22)
- *plērōma* — "fullness" (1:23); *plēroumenou* — "being filled"; *ta panta en pasin* — "all in all"/"entirely"
- *nekros* — "dead" (2:1)
- *paraptōmata / hamartiai* — "transgressions / sins" (2:1)
- *peripateō* — "walk" / behave (2:2, 2:10)
- *aiōn* — "age"/"course"/possibly a personal power (2:2)
- *archōn tēs exousias tou aeros* — "Ruler of the realm of the air" (2:2); *aēr* — "air"
- *hyioi tēs apeitheias* — "sons of disobedience"; *apeitheia* — disobedience/unbelief (2:2)
- *epithymia* — "craving" (2:3); *thelēma* — "desire" (2:3); *dianoia* — "thought" (2:3)
- *tekna physei orgēs* — "children of wrath by nature"; *physei* — "by nature/by birth" (2:3)
- *ho de theos* — "but God" (2:4); *polyeleos* / *rab-ḥesed* — "very merciful"/"abounding in steadfast love"
- *synezōopoiēsen, synēgeiren, synekathisen* — made alive/raised/seated together with (2:5–6)
- *charis* — "grace" (2:5, 8); *este sesōsmenoi* — "you are saved" (perfect periphrastic)
- *dōron* — "gift" (2:8); *dia pisteōs* — "through faith" (2:8); *ex ergōn* — "from works" (2:9)
- *poiēma* — "handiwork/creation" (2:10); *ktisthentes* — "created"; *proētoimasen* — "prepared beforehand"
- *akrobystia* — "foreskin" (2:11); *peritomē* — "circumcision"; *cheiropoiētos* — "done by hand"
- *chōris christou* — "outside Christ" (2:12); *politeia* — "way of life"/citizenship/commonwealth
- *diathēkai tēs epangelias* — "covenants of promise" (2:12); *atheoi* — "without God" (2:12)
- *makran / engys* — "far off / near" (2:13, from Isa 57:19)
- *eirēnē* — "peace" (2:14); *echthra* — "enmity" (2:14, 2:16)
- *ta amphotera / hoi amphoteroi* — "both things" (neuter, 2:14) / "both" (masculine, 2:16, 18)
- *mesotoichon* — "middle wall" (2:14); *phragmos* — "fence/hedge" (2:14)
- *en tē sarki autou* — "in his flesh" (2:14)
- *nomos tōn entolōn en dogmasin* — "law of commandments in decrees" (2:15); *katargēsas* — "setting aside"; *lysas* — "tore down"
- *heis kainos anthrōpos* — "one new human being" (2:15); *ktizō* — "create"
- *apokatallassō* — "reconcile" (2:16); *en heni sōmati* — "in one body"; *dia tou staurou* — "through the cross"; *apokteinas* — "by killing"
- *prosagōgē* — "access" (2:18); *en heni pneumati* — "in one Spirit"
- *xenoi, paroikoi, sympolitai, oikeioi* — strangers, aliens, citizens-together, household-members (2:19)
- *hagioi* — "saints" (2:19)
- *epoikodomēthentes* — "built upon" (2:20); *themelios* — "foundation"; *apostoloi kai prophētai* — apostles and prophets
- *akrogōniaios* — "most important stone"/cornerstone (2:20)
- *pasa oikodomē* — "the whole building" (2:21); *synarmologoumenē* — "being joined together"; *harmologeō* — "fit together"
- *naos hagios en kyriō* — "holy temple in the Lord" (2:21)
- *synoikodomeisthe* — "you are being built together" (2:22); *katoikētērion tou theou en pneumati* — "dwelling place of God in the Spirit"

## Overflow (past expected 2:22 endpoint) — §VI intro, 3:1–13 (lines 778–831)
FLAG: overflow beyond the assigned 1:15–2:22 scope. Introductory overview only (no verse-by-verse exegesis of ch. 3). Extracted briefly:
- 3:1–13 structure: an intercessory prayer for Gentile readers (3:1) interrupted by a digression on Paul's own commission to preach to Gentiles (3:2–13), resumed at 3:14 (*toutou charin* repeated). Frames Paul's suffering "for" (*hyper*) the Gentiles: "prisoner of Christ" (3:1), sufferings = their "glory" (3:13). *oikonomia* ("responsibility of administering") the "grace" given him = his calling to preach to Gentiles. (Thielman, ll.787–797)
- **Authorship discussion (Colossians dependence):** 3:1–13 has close verbal/thematic parallels to Col 1:23–28 (list of ~8 shared phrases at ll.803–817: *ei ge*, *egō Paulos*, *hou egenomēn diakonos*, sufferings for readers, *oikonomia*, *mystērion*=Christ, *apokekrymmenon apo tōn aiōnōn*, revealed to "his holy apostles and prophets"). Many interpreters (Mitton, Lincoln, Sterling) infer non-Pauline authorship from this dependence. **Thielman's counter:** the differences (*thlipsesin* vs *pathēmasin*; the not-quite-identical *oikonomia* line) suggest recall "from memory," not careful copying; if one doesn't concede the theological differences are "insurmountable," "there is no compelling reason to deny that Paul is the author of both." Paul "probably dictated this section of Ephesians shortly after composing Colossians." (Thielman, ll.799–825 — Thielman again defends Pauline authorship)

## Concepts / controversies fed
- **heis-kainos-anthropos** — see dedicated section (2:15): corporate new creation, new Adam replacing fallen Adam.
- **eschatological-temple** — see Temple section (2:19–22): naos, katoikētērion, akrogōniaios; multiethnic temple fulfilling Isaianic restoration (Isa 28:16; 56:3–8).
- **reconciliation** — 2:16, apokatallassō, dual (Jew/Gentile AND humanity/God), through the cross.
- **grace** — 2:5, 8–10: chariti este sesōsmenoi, dōron, not ex ergōn; realized/present salvation; imperial-benefaction background.
- **principalities-powers** — 1:20–23; 2:2: archai/exousiai/dynameis/kyriotētes; Ruler of the realm of the air; Christ enthroned above and the church sharing his victory.
- **new-creation** — 2:10 (individual, poiēma/ktisthentes) and 2:15 (corporate, ktizō).
- **ephesians-middle-wall (controversy)** — 2:14: the four positions above; Thielman = Mosaic law (Letter of Aristeas 139 parallel); temple-balustrade reading rejected; hymn theory rejected.
- Also feeds **circumcision** (2:11), **justification/works** (2:8–9 vs Rom 4–5), **Ephesians authorship controversy** (recurring: 1:22, 2:1, 2:5–6, 2:8–9, 3:1–13 — Thielman consistently argues for Pauline authorship against the pseudonymity case of Lincoln/Luz/Mitton/Sterling), **body-of-Christ / church** (1:22–23).
